definition: The system of certificate authorities, certificates, keys and processes used to issue, use and revoke certificates that tie public keys to identities.
The half of a key pair that can be given to anyone. Used to encrypt data for its owner and to verify its owner's signatures.
The half of a key pair that never leaves its owner. Used to decrypt data sent to the owner and to create the owner's signatures.
A trusted third party holds a copy of keys so that encrypted data can be recovered if a key is lost or its owner leaves.
Encryption that uses one shared key to encrypt and decrypt. Fast and suited to bulk data, but the key must be shared securely.
Encryption that uses a linked key pair: encrypt with the recipient's public key, decrypt with the recipient's private key. Slower than symmetric encryption.
Using asymmetric cryptography to set up a symmetric key, then using that symmetric key to encrypt the data. TLS works this way.
The way two parties end up with the same symmetric key over an untrusted network, for example with Diffie-Hellman.
An asymmetric key exchange algorithm. Both sides calculate the same secret from exchanged public values. It does not encrypt data.
The number of bits in a key. Longer is stronger within one algorithm; lengths cannot be compared across different algorithm families.
Advanced Encryption Standard. The current standard symmetric block cipher, with 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys.
A modern symmetric stream cipher, used as an alternative to AES.
Older symmetric ciphers that are deprecated or insecure and should be replaced with AES or ChaCha20.
An asymmetric algorithm used for encryption and digital signatures. Keys of 2048 bits are the minimum in current practice.
Elliptic curve cryptography. Asymmetric algorithms (ECDSA for signatures, ECDH for key exchange) that match RSA's strength with much shorter keys.
The current secure hash algorithm families. SHA-256 is a member of SHA-2.
Older hash algorithms that are broken for collision resistance. Do not use them for signatures or certificates.
Encrypts the whole drive, including the operating system. Protects a powered-off, lost or stolen device, not data on a running, unlocked system.
Encrypts one partition (section) of a drive, while other partitions on the same drive are left unencrypted.
Encrypts one logical drive as a unit. The volume may be a single partition, span several disks, or be a mounted container file.
Encrypts individual files or folders, often with a key tied to one user, so other users of the same computer cannot read them.
Encrypts a database's data files, logs and backups on disk. Transparent database encryption does this without changes to applications.
Encrypts individual records (rows) or fields in a database with a key the application controls, so even database administrators see ciphertext.
Encryption of data while it crosses a network (data in transit), for example with TLS or a VPN tunnel.
Transport Layer Security. Its handshake uses asymmetric cryptography to authenticate the server and agree keys; symmetric session keys then encrypt the data.
A temporary symmetric key agreed for one connection, such as a TLS session, and used to encrypt that connection's data.
A chip on the motherboard, bound to one device. Stores that device's keys, such as the disk encryption key, and supports measured boot.
A dedicated, tamper-resistant device or service that generates, stores and uses keys for many systems. The keys never leave it.
A central service that manages keys through their lifecycle: creation, rotation and revocation, with access rules and logging.
An isolated, protected processing area inside a processor or device, separate from the main operating system, for sensitive data and keys.
Making data hard to find or hard to understand. Includes steganography, tokenization and data masking.
Hiding the existence of data inside another file, such as an image, audio clip or video.
Replacing a sensitive value with a random token. The mapping is kept in a separate vault, and the token cannot be reversed by calculation.
Hiding part or all of a value from the viewer, for example showing only the last four digits of a card number.
A one-way function that turns any input into a fixed-length digest. The same input always gives the same hash. Provides integrity.
Two different inputs that produce the same hash. A hash algorithm is broken when attackers can create collisions on purpose.
Adding a unique random value to each password before hashing, so identical passwords hash differently and rainbow tables fail. The salt is not secret.
A precomputed table of hashes for likely passwords, used to look up stolen hashes. Defeated by salting.
Running a password through a deliberately slow function (bcrypt, PBKDF2, scrypt, Argon2) so that every guess is expensive for an attacker.
A hash calculated with a shared secret key. Provides integrity and authenticity, but not non-repudiation.
A hash of a message signed with the sender's private key and verified with the sender's public key. Gives integrity, authentication and non-repudiation.
A distributed, append-only ledger. Each block contains the hash of the previous block, so tampering with an earlier block is evident.
A ledger that anyone can read and verify. Provides transparency and integrity, not confidentiality.
A document that binds a public key to an identity, such as a hostname, and is digitally signed by its issuer.
An organization that checks identities and issues certificates by signing them. Root CAs sign intermediate CAs, which sign server certificates.
The starting point that is trusted without further proof, such as a root CA certificate preinstalled in a device. Everything beneath it chains to it.
A certificate issued by a public CA that browsers and operating systems already trust. Used for anything the public reaches.
A certificate signed with its own private key instead of by a CA. It can encrypt, but nothing vouches for the identity, so browsers warn.
A request sent to a CA containing the applicant's public key and identifying details, signed with the applicant's private key. The private key is never sent.
A certificate for *.example.com covers every hostname one level below the domain, such as www.example.com, but not a.b.example.com.
A signed list of the serial numbers of revoked certificates, published periodically by the CA.
A protocol for asking whether one certificate is good, revoked or unknown, in close to real time.
